paragraphs.heading: A city older than its name
paragraphs.text: Long before it was Constantinople, the place was Byzantium, a Greek colony set up in the 7th century BC. Settlers from the city-state of Megara founded it around 657 BC, facing the town of Chalcedon across the Bosphorus. Darius I brought it into the Persian Empire in 512 BC, because it sat at the narrowest point of the strait, the best spot for a floating bridge into Europe. A treaty with Rome around 150 BC traded tribute for independence, and the city then grew quietly for close to three centuries.

paragraphs.heading: Why the spot mattered
paragraphs.text: Byzantium never rivalled Athens or Sparta, but it prospered as a trading town. It stood on the land road from Europe to Asia and on the sea lane linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. It also had the Golden Horn, a roomy and excellent harbour. That position between two continents and two seas later paid for the city's palaces, domes and towers.

paragraphs.heading: New Rome
paragraphs.text: The emperor Constantine the Great refounded the city in 324 and made it the empire's new eastern capital in 330. He first called it Nova Roma, or "New Rome", and it was built on purpose to rival the old capital, with hills inside its walls said to match Rome's seven. People soon called it Constantinople instead, meaning "city of Constantine". After the western half of the empire was lost in the 5th century, it was the only capital left.

paragraphs.heading: The great city of Europe
paragraphs.text: From the middle of the 5th century to the early 13th, no city in Europe was larger or richer. It was known for Hagia Sophia, the emperors' palace, the Hippodrome and the Golden Gate. A university founded in the 5th century held an imperial library of more than 100,000 volumes. Its people, in town and in the provinces, often called it simply "the City", and that everyday phrase is where the modern name Istanbul comes from.

paragraphs.heading: Walls that held for centuries
paragraphs.text: Water on two sides, the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara, meant less ground needed walls. The Theodosian walls added a double wall about 2 kilometres west of the first one, with a moat and palisades in front. Many armies laid siege, but the defences held for nearly nine hundred years.

paragraphs.heading: Fall and afterlife
paragraphs.text: In 1204 Latin Crusaders of the Fourth Crusade sacked the city and made it capital of a short-lived Latin Empire. Byzantine forces from Nicaea won it back in 1261, but as the Ottoman state rose the empire shrank, and by the early 15th century it held little beyond the city, its surroundings and the Morea, in the Peloponnese of Greece. The Ottomans besieged and took it in 1453 and kept it as their capital until 1923, when Turkey's capital moved to Ankara. Today, as Istanbul, it is Europe's most populous city, with more than 16 million people.
